method: VHF radio-tracking (45 g VHF collars; directional 3-element Yagi antenna, triangulation where direct observation was not possible) of cage-trapped, collared cats; locations recorded a minimum of four times per night (18:00 to 05:30 h) plus random daytime locations (06:00 to 18:00 h), six consecutive days per week
conditions: Free-living leopard cats in an oil palm estate (Abstract: United Plantations/PT SSS estate; Study Site: Lada Estate), Central Kalimantan, Borneo, Indonesia; human-modified plantation habitat. 11 cats (7 males, 4 females) caught intermittently July 2014 to June 2017 in Tomahawk steel-mesh box traps baited with live rats, sedated, radio-collared and released after 3-4 h; tracked July 2014 to March 2018 (44 months), 791 independent days, 2031 locations recorded with a handheld Garmin GPS (no GPS collars). Discussion: radio-tracking 11 individuals confirmed that none were active during daytime but remained sheltered in debris rows. Pooled individuals at one estate; no camera traps. Contrast: the main row for this species from Sebangau peat forest (Jefers et al. 2019, camera traps, desk-d562) reports some daytime activity.

source.authors: Silmi M, Putra K, Amran A, Huda M, Fanani AF, Galdikas BM, Anggara SP, Traeholt C
source.title: Activity and Ranging Behavior of Leopard Cats (Prionailurus bengalensis) in an Oil Palm Landscape

quote: The cats are strictly nocturnal and prefer to hide and rest in thick bush, primarily consisting of sword-fern (Nephrolepis sp.) during day-time, but forage both on the ground and in the palm canopy at night.
note: Licence sentence read on the Frontiers PDF: 'This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).' Byline from the printed citation line (Silmi M, Putra K, Amran A, Huda M, Fanani AF, Galdikas BM, Anggara S P and Traeholt C). The paper uses the name Prionailurus bengalensis throughout, a different species name than the Mammal Diversity Database. MDD page 1006013 opened: Prionailurus javanensis (A. G. Desmarest, 1816), Sunda Leopard Cat, living, wild, 'split from P. bengalensis', countries Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, Philippines; its text names no Borneo or Kalimantan population (Sabah appears only in a photo caption), so the record is filed under P. javanensis on the split and the Indonesian range. Whole Abstract sentence, no cut. Category 'strictly nocturnal' is the paper's wording. Method is radio-telemetry, not camera trapping; no null or contrary result in the paper: it reports no diurnal activity. Different site and method from the desk-d562 Sebangau row, so not a repeat. Corrected by audit 1367 (note's MDD reading, trapping and bait in conditions).

method: camera traps (108 Bushnell Trophy Cam units at 134 randomly selected sampling sites across the four main vegetation types); activity pattern from time of records
conditions: Wild free-ranging banteng, Ujung Kulon National Park, Indonesia; 108 camera traps at 134 randomly selected sites, December 2015 to January 2017; sampling effort 46,116 camera-trap days; 817 wet-season and 644 dry-season independent records. Cameras not baited (Methods: 'We did not bait the camera'). Results: no significant deviation from a uniform activity distribution through the day in either season (Rayleigh tests, wet z=3.13, p=0.101; dry z=5.43, p=0.455, as printed), which the paper reads as suggesting the species may be cathemeral; no significant difference in day vs night encounters in either season (chi2=2.43, p=0.119; chi2=3.38, p=0.227); but banteng tended to be more active at dusk than dawn (p=0.012; mean activity time 16:42 +/- 18:48 circular stdev, as printed) and were most active in early morning and late evening (Results 3.3). Abstract: proportion of cathemeral records and recording rate did not change with protection level, moon phase or season.

value: on average more active at night than during the day
method: GPS collars with tri-axial accelerometers (e-obs); activity as overall dynamic body acceleration (ODBA) averaged over 10-minute intervals
conditions: Trapped and collared adult hares in the AgroScapeLab Quillow agricultural landscape, about 100 km north-east of Berlin (trapping described in the paper's cited earlier work; the text read does not use the words wild or free-ranging); 33 hares (11 females, 22 males) recorded in 2014, 2015, 2019 and 2020, more than 30 consecutive tracking days each within the peak reproduction period (May to August) only. Same paragraph: activity peaked around dawn and dusk, was still comparatively high at night, lowest around noon (11 AM to 2 PM); mean ODBA night 0.33 vs day 0.14 (printed '0:33' and '0:14' in the PDF text layer), 136% higher at night. The study is a weather-sensitivity analysis, not a camera-trap survey; no camera effort. Same paragraph, sex: males were on average more active than females (ODBA 0.25 vs 0.19, printed '0:25' and '0:19'), an average activity difference of 32%; model coefficient = 0.15, p < 0.001 (Table 1); sexes pooled in the value.
